study.title: Psalms 96 The Lord reigns and comes to judge the world
study.overview: Psalm 96 is a song of universal convocation: all the earth is called to worship the Lord because he is the only living God, creator of heaven, worthy of honor and fear. The psalm goes from personal and community exaltation to the public proclamation among the nations, and ends with the hope that the whole creation will rejoice before the coming of the Lord to judge with justice and truth. The text unites worship, mission, and judgment: praising God is not only an internal act, but also a testimony to the nations about his reign.

outline.title: Universal invitation to singing and ad
outline.explanation: The first three verses repeat the call to sing to the Lord. Worship is presented as a proper response to his salvation, glory, and wonders, and not as the privilege of one people. Praise must attain all the earth and all nations.

outline.title: The Lord is incomparable and worthy of reverence
outline.explanation: Here the psalmist contrasts the Lord with the idols of the peoples. He is great, fearful, creator of the heavens and clothed with majesty, glory, strength and beauty. Therefore, the families of the nations must recognize him, bring offerings and worship him with holiness and fear.

outline.title: The Lord's reign and the joy of creation
outline.explanation: The center of the proclamation is that the Lord reigns and establishes the world firmly. This truth should be announced among the nations, because their government includes fair judgment. The psalm ends with a vision of cosmic joy: heavens, earth, sea, field and trees celebrate the Lord's coming to judge with righteousness and truth.

study.context: The given notes relate the psalm to the song of praise associated with David in 1 Chronicles 16, but without requiring a unique historical conclusion about its final form. In the text itself, the focus is liturgical and missionary: Israel is called to proclaim among the nations the sovereignty of the Lord. The psalm also echoes the expectation that the reign of God will reach all peoples and all creation.
study.theology: The psalm affirms the uniqueness of God against all idolatry: the gods of the nations are nothing, but the Lord made the heavens. This establishes a theology of creation and worship: who created everything deserves all praise. There is also a theology of testimony, for the salvation of God must not be hidden, but should be proclaimed among the peoples. Finally, the final judgment does not appear as an arbitrary threat, but as a manifestation of the righteousness and truth of God, in harmony with his reign. Creation celebrating the arrival of the Lord shows that redemption and divine government reach not only people, but all created order.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm presents the universal reign of the Lord and closes with the prospect that creation enters a new order when the righteous Judge manifests.
The proclamation that the Lord reigns must be proclaimed among the nations as part of the advancement of his kingdom, and the psalm points to the inclusion of the Gentiles.
The call to sing a new song expresses praise for extraordinary works of God and summons the whole earth to exalt it.

questions: What changes in my worship when I understand that the Lord reigns over the whole earth and not just about my private life?
In what ways can I proclaim God's salvation in a concrete and daily way, as the psalm asks?
Does my reverence to God include holy fear, or has my faith been only formal and unconscious of his holiness?
study.practice: This week, turn Psalm 96 into practice: take a time to worship God with specific gratitude for his salvation; then share with someone, in a simple and respectful way, a truth about the Lord's reign and his righteousness. It is also worth observing whether his life of worship is separated from his public life: the psalm calls the believer to praise, proclaim and live in reverence. As you look at creation, let it become a reminder of God's greatness and the hope that he rules with justice.
study.uncertainty: The notes suggest links with 1 Chronicles 16 and with the expectation of the kingdom of Christ, but this remains an interpretative reading of the sources, not an explicit statement in detail by the text of this psalm. It is also not possible to confirm, only with the notes provided, questions such as authorship, accurate date or exact circumstances of the composition.
